skills.title: SI Units
skills.summary: The SI system gives everyone the same base units: the meter for length, the kilogram for mass, and the second for time.
objectives: Name the SI base unit for length, mass, and time

skills.title: Measuring Length
skills.summary: Length is measured in meters and related units. Millimeters, centimeters, meters, and kilometers scale by powers of ten.
objectives: Choose a sensible length unit for an object
Read a length measurement with its unit

skills.title: Unit Conversion
skills.summary: To convert within the metric system, multiply or divide by powers of ten: 1 meter = 100 centimeters, 1 kilogram = 1000 grams.

skills.title: Estimation and Reasonableness
skills.summary: Estimation gives a sensible approximate value and helps you check whether a measurement is reasonable.
objectives: Judge whether a measurement is reasonable

skills.title: Accuracy and Precision
skills.summary: Accuracy is how close a measurement is to the true value. Precision is how close repeated measurements are to each other. They are not the same.
objectives: Judge a set of measurements for accuracy and precision

components.body: Name the SI base units for length, mass, and time.
If everyone measures with different rulers, results cannot be compared. The SI system fixes shared units so a meter means the same thing everywhere.
SI base units: the meter (m) for length, the kilogram (kg) for mass, and the second (s) for time.
To report how far a ball rolled, use meters. To report how heavy it is, use kilograms.
SI base units: meter (length), kilogram (mass), second (time).
Choose a sensible unit and read a length with its unit.
Small things are measured in millimeters or centimeters; rooms in meters; long distances in kilometers. The unit should fit the size.
1 cm = 10 mm, 1 m = 100 cm, 1 km = 1000 m. Each step scales by a power of ten.
A pencil is about 18 cm long. A doorway is about 2 m tall. A walk to school might be 1 km.
Pick a length unit that matches the object's size, and always write the unit.
Convert between metric units by multiplying or dividing by powers of ten.
Converting does not change the amount, only the unit. 1 meter and 100 centimeters are the same length written two ways.
Convert 3 m to cm. Since 1 m = 100 cm, multiply: 3 x 100 = 300 cm.
Multiply when moving to a smaller unit (more of them) and divide when moving to a larger unit.
Metric conversions multiply or divide by 10, 100, or 1000; the amount stays the same.
Estimate everyday quantities and check if a measurement is reasonable.
An estimate is a sensible approximate value. It helps you catch mistakes: if a mouse 'weighs' 50 kg, something is wrong.
Estimate the height of a door. A typical door is about 2 m. A '2 km' door is unreasonable.
Estimate to get a sensible ballpark and to check measurements for reasonableness.
Tell accuracy and precision apart and judge measurements by both.
Accuracy is how close you are to the true value. Precision is how close repeated measurements are to each other. A measurement can be precise but not accurate.
Think of a target: accurate hits cluster on the bullseye; precise hits cluster tightly together, even if off-center.
components.accessible_text: On a target, accurate shots land near the center; precise shots land close together, which may be away from the center.

components.body: A scale reads 5.0 kg every time for a true 3.0 kg mass. It is precise (same result each time) but not accurate (far from 3.0 kg).
Getting the same answer repeatedly (precision) does not guarantee it is correct (accuracy).
Accuracy = close to true value. Precision = repeatable. They are different.

hints.text: It is the unit used on metric rulers.

questions.prompt: Why does science use shared SI units?

options: So measurements can be compared everywhere
Because they are the largest units
So each lab can use its own ruler

hints.text: Think about comparing results between people.

questions.explanation: Shared units let anyone compare measurements reliably.

questions.prompt: A scale reads 5.0 kg every time for a mass that is truly 3.0 kg. The scale is...

hints.text: Precision = same result each time. Accuracy = close to the true value.
It repeats 5.0 kg (precise) but is far from 3.0 kg (not accurate).

questions.explanation: The scale gives the same reading each time (precise) but is far from the true 3.0 kg (not accurate).

options: the same every time you repeat it

hints.text: Do not confuse this with precision (repeatability).

questions.explanation: Accuracy is closeness to the true value; repeatability is precision.
